newsitem.title: UK: Experts urge Britons to eat their veggies.
newsitem.headline: Experts urge Britons to eat their veggies.

text.p: Doctors, nutritionists and other experts joined forces on Tuesday to urge Britain, a nation of beef-eaters, to starting eating its vegetables.
The National Heart Forum said Britain should adopt the United States' "Five a Day" policy of recommending that people eat at least five servings of fruit and vegetables a day.

"It is no coincidence that this country eats little vegetables and fruit yet has one of the highest rates of coronary heart disease in the world," said cardiologist Desmond Julian, chairman of the foundation.
The U.S. policy had increased consumption there from an average of 3.9 servings a day to 4.4, the forum said.

Britons eat about half as much fruit and vegetables as the Italians and Spanish do, and have about one-third the Greek consumption. A high intake of fresh vegetables is believed to be the major factor behind the lower rates of heart disease seen in Mediterranean countries.
Michael Marmot, an expert in incidence of heart disease, said taking vitamins did not make up for the real thing.
"There is some evidence that higher intakes of vitamin C and E can help protect against heart disease," he said, but added that trials showed taking pills had no effect on death rates.

"Furthermore, there is some evidence to show that supplements of vitamin A and beta-carotene (the precursor of vitamin A) can actually increase the risk of heart disease and lung cancer, especially for smokers."

Marmot added: "In contrast, the strong message emerging from studies looking at diets rich in vegetables and fruit is that they are associated both with overall lower death rates, as well as a reduction in deaths from heart disease."

The forum, which groups 25 organisations ranging from the British Medical Association representing doctors to heart disease charities, recommended that children, especially, be urged to eat more fresh fruit and vegetables.
The British Dietetic Association said it whole-heartedly approved of the call.
"These reports further reinforce the fact that good health can't be packaged in a vitamin pill," said Lyndel Costain, spokeswoman for the association.
